A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Hypothetical Minds research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original Melting Pot evaluations, component and base-LLM ablations, and analyses of hypothesis validation.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds hyperparameter and computational-cost analyses. The separately attributed OPRE results are reused from prior work.

M1.justification: The hypothesis generation, evaluation and refinement procedure, validation rule, hierarchical planning, memory, and action planner remain unchanged. The expanded explanation and newly mentioned alternative hypothesis-selection option do not establish a change to the evaluated method; the appendix procedures and prompts are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same four Melting Pot environments and 30 scenarios: RWS Repeated, RWS Arena, Collaborative Cooking Asymmetric, and Prisoner's Dilemma. The added sensitivity and cost experiments reuse existing RWS Repeated scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds OPRE alongside the retained ReAct, Reflexion, PlanReAct, and PPO comparators throughout Figure 2 and Table 1. This introduces a hierarchical MARL comparator across all four environments, substantially strengthening the comparison set. Section 4 and Appendix E.5 explicitly identify its results as reused from Melting Pot 2.0.

E3.justification: The original benchmark protocols and defaults are retained. New experiments sweep k over 0, 1, 3, 5, and 7, and learning rate and validation threshold over 0.1–0.9. The latter use Llama3 on two unspecified representative scenarios. Appendix B also introduces cost and token measurements normalized to 1200 steps, plus episode-cost reporting at 1000 steps.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and qualitative cases, v2 adds systematic sensitivity analyses for hypothesis-memory size, learning rate, and validation threshold, together with cost-versus-reward and token-consumption analyses (Figures 11–16). These substantially extend evidence about robustness and computational tradeoffs.

E5.justification: The original five-seed benchmark reporting, SEM error bars, and three-seed base-LLM comparison remain. New figures specify SEM over 45 pooled episodes for hypothesis-count and cost analyses, and 10 episodes across two scenarios for learning-rate and threshold analyses. These extend sample-size and uncertainty reporting without establishing increased runs for existing results.

E6.justification: All existing Table 1 scores and SEM values are retained. The added OPRE column changes HM's Prisoner's Dilemma highest-mean count from five scenarios to two, with OPRE leading eight. v2 also reports new sensitivity and cost outcomes and additional full-HM scenario entries in the all-scenario ablation figure. These are added comparisons and results, not improved HM benchmark scores.

T1.justification: The partially observable Markov-game formalization, MAP expression, intrinsic-reward and Rescorla–Wagner equations, planning definitions, and appendix payoff mathematics are retained. No theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is added; the new threshold rationale and call-count discussion explain implementation.

C1.justification: The main architectural and ToM contributions remain. v2 adds an explicit first-LLM-agent claim spanning diverse social domains and qualifies MARL superiority to three of four environments in the introduction. This qualification is incomplete: the retained contribution bullet still claims superiority over RL baselines in every environment.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the earlier Prisoner's Dilemma discussion of similar heuristic play with an explanation of OPRE's advantage and HM's spatial reasoning and resource-collection limitations. It also interprets diminishing returns from larger hypothesis sets and links validation to lower costs. Existing limitations concerning manual scaffolding and supplied game rules remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 and Table 5 newly report monetary costs, episode runtimes, four-GPU Llama3 execution, and A40/L40 hardware. Section 3.2 adds LLM-call accounting and an alternative hypothesis-selection option. Model identifiers, default hyperparameters, detailed prompts, and the main repository address were already supplied in v1.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially repositioned. The cognitive-modeling review is replaced by MARL and machine-ToM discussion covering approaches such as MADDPG, MAPPO, and OPRE. v2 adds an explicit Tree-of-Thoughts comparison and broader novelty positioning, while removing discussions of several embodied-agent systems and cognitive latent-cause models. These exceed bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, ablation narrative, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Experimental subsections are reordered and framed around research questions, RWS Arena receives a separate subsection, and hyperparameters move into an earlier appendix section. Author contributions and acknowledgments are added, while much of the method and prompt text is retained.

P2.justification: v2 merges and redraws the architecture and ToM diagrams, expands the benchmark chart and table for OPRE, restores missing full-HM bars in the all-scenario ablation display, and adds six analysis figures and a cost table. The base-LLM plot moves to the appendix, and conference formatting changes typography, headers, and prompt-box layout.

improvement.justification: The hierarchical MARL comparison and new sensitivity and cost evidence make v2 more informative and easier to assess. However, important claims remain unreconciled: the contribution bullet asserts RL superiority in every environment despite OPRE's Prisoner's Dilemma advantage, and Section 4.3 retains five-of-ten scenario wins where Table 1 supports only two. The stronger evidence and practical transparency provide a limited net improvement, constrained by these reporting inconsistencies.
